entries.clue: Difficulty opposing what’s upfront? (8)

blocks.note: read 'upfront' as the up side; the opposing side faces the other way

annotation.surface: Someone wondering whether being upfront causes trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half reads 'upfront' as UP + side, so the side opposing it is the DOWN side; the question mark flags that pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A downside is a disadvantage, a difficulty that comes with something.

entries.clue: Earth cover lifted revealing some stimulating objects (6)

indicatorNotes.lifted: in a down clue, lifting the letters reads them bottom to top

blocks.note: sod is turf, a piece of earth

annotation.surface: A gardener lifting a turf cover and finding something unexpected underneath.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Earth cover' reads as one idea, a layer of turf, but it is two separate words, each giving its own chunk before the whole is flipped.
annotation.definitionFit: Dildos are sex toys, objects meant to stimulate.

entries.clue: Son immersed in drink is good for nothing (6)

indicatorNotes.immersed in: the son is dunked inside the drink, so S goes inside

blocks.note: S = son, placed between WA and TER

annotation.surface: A layabout son who spends his time drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: S is the standard abbreviation for son. 'Drink' suggests alcohol, but the drink here is plain water.
annotation.definitionFit: A waster is a good-for-nothing, someone who idles his life away.

entries.clue: Trace crime farmer reported (9)

indicatorNotes.reported: reported speech is heard, so the pieces are spoken

blocks.note: said together, sin + tiller matches the answer

annotation.surface: A detective asked to trace a crime that a farmer has reported.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trace' pretends to be a verb for police work; it is the noun meaning a tiny amount.
annotation.definitionFit: A scintilla is the tiniest trace of something, as in 'not a scintilla of evidence'.

entries.clue: Unloved, obese revolutionary is a lethal agent (6-1,5)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: the letters revolt, turning over into a new order

annotation.surface: A friendless, overweight radical who turns out to be dangerous.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface paints a far-from-suave figure; the answer is James Bond, the agent with a licence to kill.
annotation.definitionFit: Double-O Seven (007) is James Bond, whose double-O status licenses him to kill.

entries.clue: Shuts down shabby stores Scotsman has in centre (6)

indicatorNotes.has in centre: take what each word has at its centre

annotation.surface: A Scotsman's run-down shops being closed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scotsman' begs to be MAC or IAN, but here only its middle pair counts, like the other two words.
annotation.definitionFit: To abort a process is to shut it down before it finishes.

entries.clue: Graduate, as presented, is pretty ordinary (5)

blocks.note: sic means 'thus', used to mark text reproduced exactly as presented

annotation.surface: A graduate who, on first impression, seems unremarkable.
annotation.walkthrough: SIC is the Latin note editors add to show a quotation is given as it stands, errors and all.
annotation.definitionFit: Something basic is plain and no-frills, pretty ordinary.

entries.clue: Comes back with note on limits (8)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another comes first

blocks.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

annotation.surface: Someone returning with a message about restrictions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests a written message; it is a musical note, RE.
annotation.definitionFit: A ball that rebounds comes back off whatever it hits.

entries.clue: Embarrassing display by United in passage of play (5,3)

blocks.note: to make a scene is to cause an embarrassing display

annotation.surface: A football report: Manchester United players misbehaving during a spell of the match.
annotation.walkthrough: 'United' and 'passage of play' both look like football; the play is a stage play, and scene one is its opening section.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: plays divide into numbered scenes, and the first of them is one such passage.

entries.clue: Heavy drinkers they say are quite rich (8)

indicatorNotes.they say: what people say is heard, so the word is spoken

blocks.note: lushes are heavy drinkers; said aloud, it approximates the answer

annotation.surface: A claim that the big drinkers are the wealthy ones.
annotation.walkthrough: A lush is slang for a drunkard. 'Rich' looks like money, but it describes food or taste.
annotation.definitionFit: Luscious food is rich and sweet in taste.

entries.clue: Being a bit pious, a blessing can work (6)

annotation.definitionNote: a verb phrase standing for the adjective: what is usable can work

indicatorNotes.Being a bit: the answer is only a bit of the words that follow

annotation.surface: A mildly religious person hoping a blessing will do the trick.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the clue says the thing can work, the answer says it is fit to be used.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose paraphrase: the answer describes fitness for use, and the clue turns that into a phrase about functioning.

entries.clue: Keep out of sight and dodge bill (6,6)

blocks.note: a bill is a posted notice

annotation.surface: Advice for a debtor: lie low and avoid paying.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like an invoice to be dodged; it is a poster, as in 'bill-sticking'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: going unobserved is the same thing as staying hidden from view.

entries.clue: Starting out, vandal expects real trouble, that’s clear (5)

indicatorNotes.Starting: take the letter each word starts with

blocks.note: first letters of Out Vandal Expects Real Trouble

annotation.surface: A vandal setting off who is plainly heading for trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starting out' reads as one phrase, but 'out' is itself the first word of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Something overt is done openly, in clear view.

entries.clue: Price regulations Spooner said have no hope (4,5)

indicatorNotes.Spooner said: Rev. Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: price = cost; it takes the L sound from the next word
regulations = laws; it takes the C sound from the first word

annotation.surface: Price controls that Spooner thought were doomed.
annotation.walkthrough: Swap the first sounds of COST and LAWS and you get LOST CAUSE.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase names an effort already doomed, so the clue's 'no hope' is its plain meaning.

entries.clue: Unsaddle foal bucking around without warning (3,2,1,6)

indicatorNotes.bucking around: a bucking horse throws everything about, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A young horse bucking so hard it throws its saddle without warning.
annotation.walkthrough: The horse scene is complete and plausible, and the answer even fits it: a bucking foal acts all of a sudden.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the idiom describes something happening abruptly, with no advance sign.

entries.clue: The solution has four such letters – that’s not verified (9)

annotation.definition2: The solution has four such letters

blocks.clueFragment: The solution has four such letters
blocks.note: in the grid, four of this answer's nine letters are not crossed by another entry

annotation.walkthrough: A letter is 'unchecked' when no crossing entry shares it; this answer has four, in positions 2, 4, 6 and 8.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: a solver's term for uncrossed grid letters, and the everyday sense of something never examined.

entries.clue: Broadcast is copied in sequence (8)

indicatorNotes.Broadcast: to broadcast is to scatter seed, so the letters are scattered

annotation.surface: A programme that is broadcast in episodes, copied one after another.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' sounds like television and fits a series, but it works as the scatter signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Something episodic unfolds in a sequence of episodes.

entries.clue: Flat casually put together in a bright way (8)

annotation.surface: An apartment thrown together carelessly yet looking bright.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like a home; it is the adjective, as in a limp, flat performance.
annotation.definitionFit: Limpid means clear and bright, so limpidly is in a clear, bright way.

entries.clue: Unofficial book for everyone showing where the public can’t swim (7,5)

blocks.note: unofficial as in private, not public

annotation.surface: An unofficial guidebook marking the places closed to public bathers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For everyone' seems to clash with 'unofficial', but it just gives EACH.
annotation.definitionFit: A private beach is owned and closed to the public, so they cannot swim there.

entries.clue: Have a go at trendy old Italian snack (6)

blocks.note: to pan is to criticise harshly

annotation.surface: An invitation to try a fashionable old-style Italian sandwich.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Have a go at' reads as 'try'; it means attack, as a critic pans a show.
annotation.definitionFit: A panino is an Italian bread roll sandwich, the singular of panini.

entries.clue: Extremely smart acting enlivens where it’s performed (6)

indicatorNotes.Extremely: take each word's extremes, its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A theatre critic praising lively, clever acting and where it happens.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' reads as an intensifier for 'smart'; it applies to all three words.
annotation.definitionFit: Stages are the platforms on which plays are performed.

entries.clue: Wolverine perhaps making our sheep restless around river (9)

indicatorNotes.restless: restless letters will not stay in place
indicatorNotes.around: the anagram goes around the river

annotation.surface: A wolverine unsettling the farmer's flock.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface wants the wolverine to be an animal worrying sheep; it is the Marvel character, one of the X-Men.
annotation.definitionFit: Wolverine is a Marvel superhero, so 'perhaps' marks him as one example.

entries.clue: Force abandoning weapons causes annoyance (5)

indicatorNotes.abandoning: the force walks out of the word, leaving it behind

annotation.surface: An army unit laying down its arms, to someone's irritation.
annotation.walkthrough: F is the physics symbol for force.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that riles someone annoys them.

entries.clue: Meticulous old deed (5)

annotation.surface: A carefully drawn-up antique property deed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deed' suggests a legal document, but it is simply an act.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe careful precision with no detail out of place.

entries.clue: Expanding state benefit by two days is an easy task (6)

indicatorNotes.Expanding: the benefit swells to take the two days inside it

blocks.note: the dole is British slang for unemployment benefit
D = day, twice, placed inside DOLE

annotation.surface: A government extending a welfare payment by two days, and finding it simple.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Expanding' reads as the benefit being increased; instead the benefit word opens up to hold the two days.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: British informal slang for a job so simple it needs no effort.

entries.clue: Select fish for preserving (8)

blocks.note: a ling is a fish related to cod

annotation.surface: Choosing the right fish to preserve.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a kitchen instruction and the answer is exactly what the cook will do.
annotation.definitionFit: Pickling preserves food in vinegar or brine.

entries.clue: Most reluctant to give positive response in bed (6)

indicatorNotes.in: the response sits in the bed

blocks.note: yes is a positive response, placed between CO and T

annotation.surface: Someone shy about saying yes in the bedroom.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is saucy, and the answer suits it: the coyest person is slowest to say yes.
annotation.definitionFit: Coy means reluctantly shy, so the coyest is the most reluctant.

entries.clue: Useless criminal sheds load, dumping heroin (8)

annotation.definitionNote: an adjective standing for a noun: a dead loss is someone useless

indicatorNotes.criminal: a criminal version of the letters is a corrupted one
indicatorNotes.dumping: dumping the heroin drops its letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder once the H is gone
H = heroin, dumped from the fodder

annotation.surface: A hopeless criminal ditching his drug consignment.
annotation.walkthrough: H is street slang for heroin. Remove it from SHEDSLOAD and rearrange the eight letters left.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: British informal for a person or thing that is of no use at all, so the adjective stands in for it.
